title: The Iwakura Mission
text:
In late 1871, only a few years after the Meiji Restoration, Japan's new government sent abroad an extraordinary delegation. It was led by Iwakura Tomomi, a senior court noble, with several of the country's most powerful leaders as deputies, including Okubo Toshimichi, Kido Takayoshi and the young Ito Hirobumi. Dozens of officials went with them, along with students who would stay abroad to study, among them a handful of young girls.

The mission had two aims. The first was to begin revising the unequal treaties that Western powers had forced on Japan. That failed quickly: in the United States the envoys found they were not ready to negotiate on equal terms. The second aim became the real work: to see how the Western world functioned and what Japan should learn.

For nearly two years the delegation traveled through the United States and Europe, visiting Britain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, Russia, Scandinavia, Italy, Austria and Switzerland. They divided their attention among constitutions, parliaments, schools, factories, shipyards, railways, banks, prisons and armies, and compared notes. The historian Kume Kunitake kept a detailed record, later published in five volumes.

The leaders returned in 1873 convinced that Japan needed above all to strengthen itself at home, building industry, education and modern institutions. They opposed a proposal to send an expedition against Korea and focused on reform. Many of the policies that transformed Meiji Japan grew from what they had seen together.
lesson: A team sent out to learn, and willing to share and compare what each member sees, can bring back what an organization needs. Learning together builds shared conviction.
people: Iwakura Tomomi, Okubo Toshimichi, Kido Takayoshi, Ito Hirobumi, Kume Kunitake
location: United States and Europe; Tokyo, Japan
source: Kume Kunitake, The Iwakura Embassy, 1871 to 1873: A True Account of the Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary's Journey of Observation through the United States and Europe (1878; English translation 2002)
